analysis.one_liner: Limits Medicare, Medicaid, and veterans' drug coverage to generic medicines made in the United States.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee in July 2023 and never received a markup, vote, or floor action before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, and Department of Veterans Affairs health programs from paying for generic drugs made in other countries, unless a drug has fewer than two versions made domestically, the domestic versions are in shortage or being discontinued, or the Health Secretary decides access is essential [S2, S3]. It would also let the FDA speed up review of new generic applications for drugs that lack at least two domestic generic makers [S2, S3]. The stated aim is to rebuild domestic generic drug manufacturing and reduce dependence on foreign supply chains. The bill never got a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic generic drug manufacturers gain a guaranteed, federally funded market: once at least two U.S.-made generic versions of a drug exist, federal programs could only buy those versions, excluding cheaper foreign-made competitors [S2, S3]. Patients in federal health programs could gain more reliable supplies if manufacturing moves onshore, since recent generic shortages have been linked to foreign production concentrated in a few overseas plants (general knowledge). The FDA fast-track provision could bring new domestic generic competitors to market sooner for drugs that currently have few or none made here [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Beginning January 1, 2025, Medicare Part B and Part D would pay only for generic drugs manufactured domestically, with exceptions for shortage, discontinuation, or when the Secretary deems access essential [S3].

Medicaid and CHIP would exclude foreign-made generics when a domestically made generic referencing the same brand drug exists, and VA and DOD procurement would be restricted to domestically made generics with the same exceptions [S2, S3].

The FDA could expedite development and review of generic applications for brand-name drugs that lack at least two domestically manufactured generic versions, including senior-manager involvement and a cross-disciplinary review lead [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal health programs, and ultimately taxpayers and beneficiaries, would likely bear higher drug costs: a large share of the U.S. generic supply is made abroad, largely in India and China, where lower production costs keep generic prices among the world's lowest; forcing federal purchases onto higher-cost domestic production would raise what Medicare, Medicaid, and the VA pay (general knowledge about how generic manufacturing and pricing work, applied to the mandate in [S2, S3]). Foreign-made generic manufacturers would lose their federal program sales. Patients could also face gaps if domestic manufacturers cannot ramp up capacity quickly, though the bill's shortage and essential-access exceptions are designed to catch those cases [S3].

drawbacks.text: The coverage ban could raise costs for Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal programs, because generic prices are low largely due to foreign competition, and the bill gives domestic makers a protected market once two U.S.-made versions exist [S2, S3].

The bill's protection depends on the government correctly identifying which drugs have at least two domestic generic makers; if domestic capacity proves slower or costlier to build than expected, patients could face access problems, cushioned only by case-by-case exceptions that require the Health Secretary to act drug by drug [S3].
The bill was never scored or debated in committee, so its actual effects on shortages, prices, and supply security were never tested in the legislative process [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — reducing reliance on foreign drug manufacturing after years of well-publicized generic shortages — is legitimate and has genuine public-health value. But a hard payment ban with carve-outs is a blunt instrument: it hands domestic generic makers a protected market first and hopes supply resilience follows, while the near-term costs (higher program spending, transition gaps) land on federal programs and patients. A more targeted approach, such as stockpiling or purchase guarantees for shortage-prone drugs, could have pursued the same goal with less price risk. Since the bill never advanced, no trade-off was ever formally weighed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in July 2023, and the committee never took it up before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Rick Scott (R-FL) introduced the AMERICAN DRUGS Act on July 27, 2023 [S1, S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; that was the last action recorded [S5].
Two Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democratic senator did [S4].
The committee never scheduled a markup or vote, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign-made generic manufacturers kept full access to Medicare, Medicaid, VA, and TRICARE sales, and federal health programs kept buying generics at the lower prices foreign competition supports. Domestic generic makers gained nothing, and the shortage-resilience goal the bill pursued went unaddressed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Foreign generic makers and federal drug budgets

for.name: Sen. Rick Scott
for.role: U.S. Senator from Florida; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the HELP Committee.

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a committee markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported it, but the bill also drew no recorded opposition — it simply died in committee without a vote, so the partisan shape was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would make federally funded coverage flow exclusively through domestically made generics once two U.S. versions exist, giving these manufacturers a protected market that foreign competitors are barred from serving. They would also benefit from expedited FDA review for drugs lacking domestic competition. Their gain is protection from cheaper foreign rivals, though they would also supply the redundancy the bill's shortage-resilience goal depends on.

industries.industry: Foreign-made generic drug manufacturers (largely India and China)
industries.note: The bill would exclude their products from Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, VA, and TRICARE whenever domestic versions exist. Their cheaper generic drugs are a large part of why U.S. generic prices are low, so losing federal program access would come at patients' and programs' expense.

The FDA fast-track would accelerate generic competition for brand-name drugs that have fewer than two domestically made generic versions, modestly eroding their market exclusivity. The coverage mandate itself does not target them.
